title: The Hunter in the Bilva Tree
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hookLine: the hunter in the bilva tree can't afford to sleep, and the deer start coming
carry: jagarana: shiva's night is kept awake, together
tomorrow: why say the same five syllables all night?

cards: Back to yesterday's hunter. The Shiva Purana gives him a name, Gurudruha, and a reason to be in that tree: his family is hungry, and he can't go home empty-handed.
So he sits on a branch above the pool with his pot of water and his bow, waiting for animals to come and drink. He doesn't sleep; he can't afford to.
He has no idea that tonight is the great night of Shiva, or that the stone in the roots below him is a linga. The night is long, and he is about to have visitors.

teach.h: A DOE: LET ME GO, I'LL COME BACK.
teach.b: In the first watch of the night, a doe comes down to the water. He draws his bow. And the doe speaks: let me go home first and leave my little ones safe, and i promise i'll come back to you.

Hungry as he is, he lets her go. Later another doe comes, then a stag, each with the same plea, each let go on a promise. So the hunter sits on his branch, hour after hour, awake, waiting for deer who may never return.
What was happening below him, we'll come to. Today, look at the waking itself.

Keeping awake on this night is called jagarana, the vigil, and it's one of the main things Hindus do on Maha Shivaratri. The hunter stayed up for his own reasons, and in the Shiva Purana the night still counted for him.
Families who keep it on purpose add two things he didn't have. First, company.
In temples the night is cut into four watches, each with its own worship, with bhajans and Om Namah Shivaya in between, so there's always something to wake into.
Second, a direction: not just awake, awake toward Shiva. Many teachers read the body's vigil as a rehearsal for the other waking, the one the Katha Upanishad calls for: arise, awake, and learn.

If you've ever sat up with family through a long night, at a hospital, a wedding, a wake, you know how it works: nobody keeps the night alone. Shivaratri turns that into worship, and points it at Shiva.

how: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus who keep the jagarana stay awake through the night, in temples or at home, with bhajans, chanting of Om Namah Shivaya, and rounds of worship of the linga until dawn.

s: the vigil is mainly a contest to see who can last
it's kept together and on purpose, awake toward Shiva, not just awake.
in the Shiva Purana, a hunter keeps Shivaratri awake without meaning to
Gurudruha sat up all night in a bilva tree waiting for deer, and the night still counted for him.
in temples, the night is kept in total silence
it's held up by singing, chanting and the worship of each watch, so there's always something to wake into.

games.q: it's two in the morning in the temple courtyard. the person beside you keeps nodding off. what do you do?
o: let them sleep; it's their vow, not yours.
start the next song, or sing it with them.
slip out quietly so you don't disturb anyone.
games.why: on this night wakefulness is shared. nobody stays up by their own strength alone, and a song is how a tired crowd lifts its head.

practice: Sit a little straighter than usual, eyes just slightly open and resting on a spot in front of you, and when the mind starts to drift or dull, the way heads nod at two in the morning, don't scold yourself.

Lift: straighten the back, take one fuller breath, and come back, because every lift is a small vigil. If you pray, you can let Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, be the song that lifts you.
